title: ISS608-VAA
text:
Cover


Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility


ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1 · Visual Analytics for Data Discovery


Cheng Yuanyuan · 23 May 2026



This executive summary uses the same motor insurance portfolio data, but applies a different visual analytics path from the earlier version. The focus is on distribution, concentration, pricing adequacy, and exposure-adjusted segment comparison. The slide deck is designed to support management decisions rather than only describe variables.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Observation 1 — The dataset is large enough for exposure-adjusted portfolio analysis
text:
Observation 1 — The dataset is large enough for exposure-adjusted portfolio analysis



The portfolio contains 354,140 policy-year records and 185,678 insured IDs.
Exposure is explicitly available, so comparisons should be made using premium/exposure, claims/exposure, and incurred/exposure, not raw totals alone.
Implication: the dataset supports credible portfolio-level visual analytics, provided segment comparisons are exposure-adjusted.



This slide checks whether the data structure supports the assignment purpose. The key issue is that policy records do not all represent identical exposure. Therefore, the analysis uses exposure-weighted measures. The missingness plot is included because variables with high missingness should not be used for strong causal claims without caution.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Analytical Framework — Separate volume, price, frequency, severity and tail risk
text:
Analytical Framework — Separate volume, price, frequency, severity and tail risk


Pricing adequacyPortfolio loss ratio = incurred / premium. This is the main profitability metric.


Claim frequencyClaims / exposure identifies how often adverse events occur.


Claim severityIncurred / claim separates expensive claims from frequent claims.




Exposure baseExposure prevents small segments from being overinterpreted.


Tail volatilityECDF and Pareto views reveal concentration not visible in averages.


ValidationTests and model diagnostics check whether visual differences persist statistically.



The analysis deliberately avoids treating average loss ratio as a sufficient answer. Insurance profitability is skewed, zero-heavy, and segment-dependent.


The framework follows an actuarial logic. Loss ratio explains premium adequacy, but it does not tell whether the problem comes from claim frequency or severity. Exposure matters because small groups can look extreme simply by chance. The selected methods therefore combine distribution plots, concentration analysis, segment charts, heatmaps, and statistical checks.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Observation 2 — Premium and incurred cost move differently over time
text:
Observation 2 — Premium and incurred cost move differently over time



Indexed trends show whether premium rate, incurred cost, claim frequency, and loss ratio move together or diverge.
Implication: if incurred cost rises faster than premium rate, portfolio growth is not automatically profitable.



This chart is chosen instead of four separate bar charts because indexing allows direct comparison of metrics with different units. It shows whether premium, claims, and loss ratio are moving in the same direction. For management, the key point is the relative movement, not the raw accounting totals.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Observation 3 — Loss experience is zero-heavy and strongly right-skewed
text:
Observation 3 — Loss experience is zero-heavy and strongly right-skewed



ECDFs are more suitable than normal curves because most policy-years have no claims or no incurred loss.
Implication: averages alone are unstable; later segment comparisons should use capped distributions and portfolio-weighted summaries.



This slide uses ECDFs because they show the full cumulative distribution without assuming normality. Histograms would be dominated by the spike near zero, while ECDFs still show the long right tail. The zero-share bar makes the zero-heavy structure explicit.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 1 — A small tail of policy-years contributes a large share of incurred losses
text:
Insight 1 — A small tail of policy-years contributes a large share of incurred losses



The Pareto curve shows whether losses are broadly distributed or concentrated in a small adverse tail.
Implication: volatility management should focus on tail exposure, not only average segment performance.



A Pareto curve is used because insurance losses are often concentrated. This view is more decision-useful than a single mean or median because it tells management whether most losses come from many ordinary policies or a small tail of severe outcomes.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 2 — Premium level does not fully explain incurred loss
text:
Insight 2 — Premium level does not fully explain incurred loss



The binned density view avoids overplotting hundreds of thousands of policy-years.
Implication: pricing review should look for clusters above the break-even line, where incurred loss exceeds premium.



A normal scatterplot would be unreadable because the dataset is large. A binned heatmap preserves the relationship between premium and incurred loss while showing where records are concentrated. The dashed line provides an intuitive profitability reference.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 3 — Product type remains a primary profitability separator
text:
Insight 3 — Product type remains a primary profitability separator



Product comparisons use portfolio-weighted loss ratio and exposure share together.
Implication: a high loss ratio is more urgent when the product also carries meaningful exposure.



A lollipop plot is used instead of a bar chart to emphasise relative ranking without visually overloading the slide. Exposure share is shown beside the loss ratio because management should not treat a tiny product and a large product as equally important.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 4 — Bonus score separates risk, but distributions overlap
text:
Insight 4 — Bonus score separates risk, but distributions overlap



Violin + boxplot shows both distribution shape and median/IQR, rather than hiding overlap behind one average.
Implication: bonus score is useful, but it should be combined with other underwriting variables.



This chart was selected because a pure bar chart would imply each bonus group is homogeneous. The violin layer shows distribution spread, while the boxplot gives a familiar summary. The paired claim-frequency chart helps separate how often claims happen from how large the resulting losses are.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 5 — Payment and business context change risk mix
text:
Insight 5 — Payment and business context change risk mix



The heatmap shows combined effects rather than evaluating payment frequency alone.
Implication: payment behaviour should be interpreted together with business context before repricing.



A two-way heatmap is selected because payment frequency and business type may interact. This is better than separate one-variable bar charts, which can hide combined risk pockets. The line chart then shows whether differences are driven by claim frequency.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 6 — Vehicle brand outliers require exposure-aware screening
text:
Insight 6 — Vehicle brand outliers require exposure-aware screening



Funnel plot avoids overreacting to small brands with unstable loss ratios.
Implication: brands above the exposure-adjusted band deserve deeper underwriting review.



This chart is chosen because brand groups have unequal exposure. A simple ranked bar chart would overstate small-exposure outliers. A funnel plot is more defensible because it compares segment loss ratio against exposure-adjusted tolerance bands.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Insight 7 — Vehicle value and power create interaction-based risk pockets
text:
Insight 7 — Vehicle value and power create interaction-based risk pockets



Interaction heatmap shows risk pockets that one-variable charts cannot identify.
Implication: vehicle pricing should monitor combinations, not only independent variables.



The heatmap is selected because the management question is about combinations of characteristics. Vehicle value or power alone may not reveal the highest-risk cells. Filtering out low-exposure cells avoids giving too much attention to unstable small groups.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Method Add-on — Distribution shapes differ by product and bonus group
text:
Method Add-on — Distribution shapes differ by product and bonus group



Density and quantile-profile views expose distribution shape, not only central tendency.
Implication: the best pricing signal is not only which group has the highest mean, but which group has a thicker adverse tail.



This is the advanced visual analytics add-on. It uses distribution-shape diagnostics rather than another simple bar chart. The density chart compares product-level shape, while the quantile profile shows how groups diverge across the distribution, including the upper tail.

title: ISS608-VAA
section: Statistical Validation — Visual differences are checked formally
text:
Statistical Validation — Visual differences are checked formally



Non-parametric validation is used because capped loss ratio is still skewed and non-normal.
Implication: visual findings are not presented as decoration; they are checked against statistical evidence.



The Kruskal-Wallis test is used because the outcome distribution is skewed and has many zeros. The purpose is not to replace visual analytics, but to check whether the visual segment differences are statistically visible. A claim-occurrence chart adds a frequency-side validation.

title: ISS608-VAA
text:
Final Recommendations

1. Price by exposure-adjusted loss ratio, not raw incurred totals.Loss ratio is the main portfolio profitability metric, but it must be interpreted with exposure.


2. Separate frequency risk from severity risk.High claim frequency and high incurred severity point to different underwriting actions.


3. Prioritise product and bonus-score review.These variables create visible profitability separation and should enter the first pricing shortlist.


4. Use funnel screening before acting on small segments.Extreme loss ratios in low-exposure brands can be noise; funnel plots provide a more defensible signal.


5. Monitor interaction pockets.Vehicle value × power-to-weight combinations reveal risk pockets that single-variable summaries can miss.


Overall conclusion: profitability pressure is not random. It is concentrated in observable product, bonus, payment, vehicle, and brand-risk structures. The next step should be actuarial modelling, but the visual analytics already identifies where management attention should begin.


The recommendations translate the visual analysis into decision rules. The strongest practical conclusion is that management should not use one overall loss ratio alone. It should separate pricing adequacy, frequency, severity, exposure size, and interaction pockets before repricing or underwriting intervention.

title: Hands-on_Ex05a
text:
In this exercise, we learn how to visualise data distribution using two methods: ridgeline plot and raincloud plot.
A ridgeline plot is useful when we want to compare the distribution of one numeric variable across many groups. A raincloud plot is useful because it combines density shape, boxplot summary, and individual data points in one chart.
By the end of this exercise, we should be able to:

create ridgeline plots using ggridges;
create raincloud plots using ggdist;
compare distribution shapes across different groups;
explain what the chart tells us.







pacman::p_load(ggdist, ggridges, ggthemes,
               colorspace, tidyverse)





exam <- read_csv("../data/Exam_data.csv")

Rows: 322 Columns: 7
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (4): ID, CLASS, GENDER, RACE
dbl (3): ENGLISH, MATHS, SCIENCE

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.



glimpse(exam)

Rows: 322
Columns: 7
$ ID      <chr> "Student321", "Student305", "Student289", "Student227", "Stude…
$ CLASS   <chr> "3I", "3I", "3H", "3F", "3I", "3I", "3I", "3I", "3I", "3H", "3…
$ GENDER  <chr> "Male", "Female", "Male", "Male", "Male", "Female", "Male", "M…
$ RACE    <chr> "Malay", "Malay", "Chinese", "Chinese", "Malay", "Malay", "Chi…
$ ENGLISH <dbl> 21, 24, 26, 27, 27, 31, 31, 31, 33, 34, 34, 36, 36, 36, 37, 38…
$ MATHS   <dbl> 9, 22, 16, 77, 11, 16, 21, 18, 19, 49, 39, 35, 23, 36, 49, 30,…
$ SCIENCE <dbl> 15, 16, 16, 31, 25, 16, 25, 27, 15, 37, 42, 22, 32, 36, 35, 45…



summary(exam$ENGLISH)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   59.00   70.00   67.18   78.00   96.00 






A ridgeline plot is useful when the same numeric variable needs to be compared across multiple groups. In this example, the English score distribution is compared across different classes.
The advantage of this method is that it keeps all classes on one shared x-axis, making it easier to compare the shape, centre and spread of each class distribution.


The basic ridgeline plot can be created using geom_density_ridges(). Here, ENGLISH is placed on the x-axis and CLASS is placed on the y-axis.
The fill colour is adjusted to a muted teal tone to make the plot look cleaner and more consistent with the overall website style.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.2,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English scores",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.4))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of English Scores by Class",
    subtitle = "Ridgeline plot allows multiple class distributions to be compared together"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )











ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.2,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English scores",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.4))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of English Scores by Class",
    subtitle = "Ridgeline plot allows multiple class distributions to be compared together"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




From this plot, we can compare whether some classes have more concentrated English scores while others show wider score variation. A taller or sharper ridge usually suggests that many students are clustered around a similar score range.



Instead of filling each ridge with one fixed colour, we can allow the colour to change along the x-axis. This is done using geom_density_ridges_gradient().
This version makes the score direction more visible because lower and higher English scores are represented by different colour intensity.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "English score",
    option = "C"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English scores",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.4))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gradient Ridgeline Plot of English Scores",
    subtitle = "Colour changes along the score axis to highlight lower and higher score ranges"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "English score",
    option = "C"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English scores",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.4))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gradient Ridgeline Plot of English Scores",
    subtitle = "Colour changes along the score axis to highlight lower and higher score ranges"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




This plot is useful when the audience needs to quickly identify where low, middle and high scores appear in each class distribution.



Another way to colour a ridgeline plot is to map the empirical cumulative distribution function, also known as ECDF, onto the fill colour. This helps highlight the central region and tail areas of the distribution.
In the code below, calc_ecdf = TRUE is important because it tells stat_density_ridges() to calculate ECDF-related values.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5 - after_stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Tail probability",
    option = "D",
    direction = -1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Probability-based Colouring",
    subtitle = "The colour scale helps separate central values from distribution tails"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5 - after_stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Tail probability",
    option = "D",
    direction = -1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Probability-based Colouring",
    subtitle = "The colour scale helps separate central values from distribution tails"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )










Important



The argument calc_ecdf = TRUE should not be removed. Without it, the ECDF-based colour mapping will not work properly.





Quantile lines can be added to show how the distribution is divided into different sections. In the example below, the distribution is divided into four quartiles.
This makes the ridgeline plot more informative because it shows not only the density shape, but also the internal score segmentation.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    name = "Quartiles",
    option = "C"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Quartile Lines",
    subtitle = "Quartile lines divide each class distribution into four score sections"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    name = "Quartiles",
    option = "C"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Quartile Lines",
    subtitle = "Quartile lines divide each class distribution into four score sections"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




We can also define the quantiles manually. The next chart separates the lower tail, middle range and upper tail using 2.5% and 97.5% cut points.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#D95F02A0", "#2A6F6FA0", "#7570B3A0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Tail Probability Cut Points",
    subtitle = "Lower and upper tails are separated from the main score range"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#D95F02A0", "#2A6F6FA0", "#7570B3A0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Tail Probability Cut Points",
    subtitle = "Lower and upper tails are separated from the main score range"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




This version is useful when the analysis is more interested in extreme score ranges, such as unusually low or unusually high English scores.




A raincloud plot combines three layers:

a half-density plot showing the distribution shape;
a boxplot showing median and interquartile range;
dots showing individual observations.

Compared with a normal boxplot, a raincloud plot gives a fuller view because it shows both summary statistics and the actual data pattern.
In this section, the English score distribution is compared across different race groups.


The first layer is created using stat_halfeye() from the ggdist package. It produces a half-density shape.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-eye Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "The half-density layer shows the distribution shape for each group",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()











ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-eye Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "The half-density layer shows the distribution shape for each group",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










Tip



Setting .width = 0 and point_colour = NA removes the interval and point marker, leaving a cleaner half-density shape.





Next, a narrow boxplot is added on top of the half-eye layer. The boxplot provides a compact summary of the median, lower quartile and upper quartile.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = .18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.55,
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-eye Plot with Boxplot Layer",
    subtitle = "The boxplot adds a statistical summary to the distribution shape",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()











ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = .18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.55,
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-eye Plot with Boxplot Layer",

    x = "Race",

The third layer adds dots to represent individual observations. This makes the plot less abstract because the viewer can see the actual data points behind the distribution.

Finally, coord_flip() is used to turn the chart horizontally. This makes the raincloud shape easier to read and gives more space for group labels.
A clean minimal theme is used here instead of a heavy publication theme, so the chart looks more modern and consistent with the customised colourway.

title: Hands-on_Ex05a
text:
A ridgeline plot is useful when the same numeric variable needs to be compared across multiple groups. In this example, the English score distribution is compared across different classes.
The advantage of this method is that it keeps all classes on one shared x-axis, making it easier to compare the shape, centre and spread of each class distribution.


The basic ridgeline plot can be created using geom_density_ridges(). Here, ENGLISH is placed on the x-axis and CLASS is placed on the y-axis.
The fill colour is adjusted to a muted teal tone to make the plot look cleaner and more consistent with the overall website style.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.2,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English scores",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.4))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of English Scores by Class",
    subtitle = "Ridgeline plot allows multiple class distributions to be compared together"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )











ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.2,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English scores",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.4))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of English Scores by Class",
    subtitle = "Ridgeline plot allows multiple class distributions to be compared together"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




From this plot, we can compare whether some classes have more concentrated English scores while others show wider score variation. A taller or sharper ridge usually suggests that many students are clustered around a similar score range.



Instead of filling each ridge with one fixed colour, we can allow the colour to change along the x-axis. This is done using geom_density_ridges_gradient().
This version makes the score direction more visible because lower and higher English scores are represented by different colour intensity.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "English score",
    option = "C"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English scores",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.4))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gradient Ridgeline Plot of English Scores",
    subtitle = "Colour changes along the score axis to highlight lower and higher score ranges"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "English score",
    option = "C"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English scores",
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(
    name = NULL,
    expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.4))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Gradient Ridgeline Plot of English Scores",
    subtitle = "Colour changes along the score axis to highlight lower and higher score ranges"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




This plot is useful when the audience needs to quickly identify where low, middle and high scores appear in each class distribution.



Another way to colour a ridgeline plot is to map the empirical cumulative distribution function, also known as ECDF, onto the fill colour. This helps highlight the central region and tail areas of the distribution.
In the code below, calc_ecdf = TRUE is important because it tells stat_density_ridges() to calculate ECDF-related values.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5 - after_stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Tail probability",
    option = "D",
    direction = -1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Probability-based Colouring",
    subtitle = "The colour scale helps separate central values from distribution tails"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5 - after_stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Tail probability",
    option = "D",
    direction = -1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Probability-based Colouring",
    subtitle = "The colour scale helps separate central values from distribution tails"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )










Important



The argument calc_ecdf = TRUE should not be removed. Without it, the ECDF-based colour mapping will not work properly.





Quantile lines can be added to show how the distribution is divided into different sections. In the example below, the distribution is divided into four quartiles.
This makes the ridgeline plot more informative because it shows not only the density shape, but also the internal score segmentation.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    name = "Quartiles",
    option = "C"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Quartile Lines",
    subtitle = "Quartile lines divide each class distribution into four score sections"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(
    name = "Quartiles",
    option = "C"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Quartile Lines",
    subtitle = "Quartile lines divide each class distribution into four score sections"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




We can also define the quantiles manually. The next chart separates the lower tail, middle range and upper tail using 2.5% and 97.5% cut points.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#D95F02A0", "#2A6F6FA0", "#7570B3A0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Tail Probability Cut Points",
    subtitle = "Lower and upper tails are separated from the main score range"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(after_stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),
    scale = 2.8,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#D95F02A0", "#2A6F6FA0", "#7570B3A0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ridgeline Plot with Tail Probability Cut Points",
    subtitle = "Lower and upper tails are separated from the main score range"
  ) +
  theme_ridges() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




This version is useful when the analysis is more interested in extreme score ranges, such as unusually low or unusually high English scores.

text:
A raincloud plot combines three layers:

a half-density plot showing the distribution shape;
a boxplot showing median and interquartile range;
dots showing individual observations.

Compared with a normal boxplot, a raincloud plot gives a fuller view because it shows both summary statistics and the actual data pattern.
In this section, the English score distribution is compared across different race groups.


The first layer is created using stat_halfeye() from the ggdist package. It produces a half-density shape.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-eye Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "The half-density layer shows the distribution shape for each group",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()











ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Half-eye Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "The half-density layer shows the distribution shape for each group",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










Tip



Setting .width = 0 and point_colour = NA removes the interval and point marker, leaving a cleaner half-density shape.





Next, a narrow boxplot is added on top of the half-eye layer. The boxplot provides a compact summary of the median, lower quartile and upper quartile.

    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = .18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.55,
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.15,
    binwidth = .5,
    dotsize = 1.6,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    fill = "#F2A65A"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud Plot with Dot Layer",
    subtitle = "Dots show the individual observations within each race group",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()




This layer is useful because it prevents the chart from hiding the sample size and the actual spread of observations.



Finally, coord_flip() is used to turn the chart horizontally. This makes the raincloud shape easier to read and gives more space for group labels.
A clean minimal theme is used here instead of a heavy publication theme, so the chart looks more modern and consistent with the customised colourway.

The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = .18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.55,
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.15,
    binwidth = .5,
    dotsize = 1.45,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    fill = "#F2A65A"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "Density, boxplot and individual dots are combined in one chart",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

  arguments of `?ggdist::geom_dots()` or the section on constraining dot sizes
  in vignette("dotsinterval") (`vignette(ggdist::dotsinterval)`).












ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = RACE,
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5,
    justification = -0.25,
    .width = 0,
    point_colour = NA,
    fill = lighten("#2A6F6F", .35),
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = .18,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.55,
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  stat_dots(
    side = "left",
    justification = 1.15,
    binwidth = .5,
    dotsize = 1.45,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    fill = "#F2A65A"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Raincloud Plot of English Scores by Race",
    subtitle = "Density, boxplot and individual dots are combined in one chart",
    x = "Race",
    y = "English scores"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )







To add a small extension beyond the original tutorial, we can calculate the median English score for each race group. This provides a simple numerical check to support the visual comparison made in the raincloud plot.

race_summary <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_english = mean(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_english = median(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_english = sd(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

race_summary

  RACE        n mean_english median_english sd_english
  <chr>   <int>        <dbl>          <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Chinese   193         70.8             73       13.2
2 Indian     12         60.8             59       16.8
3 Malay     108         61.3             64       15.2
4 Others      9         70.1             70       14.0



The plotThe code chunk



ggplot(race_summary,
       aes(x = reorder(RACE, median_english),
           y = median_english)) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(median_english, 1)),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Median English score",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median English Score by Race",
    subtitle = "A simple summary chart to support the raincloud plot interpretation",
    x = "Race"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )











race_summary <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_english = mean(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_english = median(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_english = sd(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ggplot(race_summary,
       aes(x = reorder(RACE, median_english),
           y = median_english)) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(median_english, 1)),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Median English score",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median English Score by Race",
    subtitle = "A simple summary chart to support the raincloud plot interpretation",
    x = "Race"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )




This extension is intentionally simple. The raincloud plot shows the full distribution, while the median bar chart gives a quick business-style summary. Used together, they make the interpretation clearer without making the exercise too complicated.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
This hands-on exercise focuses on learning how to construct statistical graphics using the Layered Grammar of Graphics in ggplot2. The exercise uses the Exam_data dataset to demonstrate how different graphical layers, aesthetic mappings, geometric objects, statistical transformations, faceting, coordinates, and themes can be combined to produce clear and meaningful visualisations.
The main objective is not only to reproduce the charts from the tutorial, but also to understand how each ggplot2 component contributes to the final visual output.

section: 2.2 Introducing ggplot2: Distribution of Students by Race
text:
2.2 Introducing ggplot2: Distribution of Students by Race
ggplot2 is an R package for declaratively creating data-driven graphics based on The Grammar of Graphics.
It is also part of the tidyverse family specially designed for visual exploration and communication.
For more detail, visit ggplot2 link.o(^_-)O

2.2.1 Basic Bar Chart Using geom_bar()
The first visualisation is a simple bar chart showing the distribution of students by race. Since RACE is a categorical variable, geom_bar() is suitable because it counts the number of observations in each category automatically.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) + 
  geom_bar()











2.2.2 Improving the Bar Chart Design
The basic bar chart correctly shows the distribution of students by race, but the default ggplot2 style can be improved. The following version adds a clearer title, axis labels, a cleaner theme, and a more intentional colour design.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE, fill = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(width = 0.65) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Students by Race",
    subtitle = "Based on the Exam_data dataset",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









From the improved bar chart, Chinese students form the largest group in the dataset, followed by Malay students. Indian students and students classified under Others make up much smaller groups. This indicates that the dataset is not evenly distributed across race categories, which should be considered when interpreting later comparisons by race.


2.2.3 Aesthetic Mapping versus Fixed Aesthetic
In ggplot2, aesthetics can be controlled in two different ways. If an aesthetic such as fill is placed inside aes(), it is mapped to a variable in the dataset. If it is placed outside aes(), it is applied as a fixed visual setting.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.65) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Students by Race with Fixed Fill Colour",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









Unlike the previous improved bar chart, this version uses a fixed fill colour. The colour is not linked to the RACE variable, so all bars share the same colour. This is useful when the purpose is to compare bar heights without using colour to represent categories.


2.2.4 Comparing geom_bar() and geom_col()
geom_bar() is used when the dataset contains raw observations and ggplot2 needs to count the number of rows in each category. In contrast, geom_col() is used when the dataset already contains summarised values.


Code
race_count <- exam_data %>%
  count(RACE)

race_count


# A tibble: 4 × 2
  RACE        n
  <chr>   <int>
1 Chinese   193
2 Indian     12
3 Malay     108
4 Others      9


The summarised table can now be visualised using geom_col(). Unlike geom_bar(), geom_col() does not count rows automatically. Instead, it uses the pre-calculated n column as the height of each bar.


Code
ggplot(data = race_count,
       aes(x = RACE, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2A6F6F", color = "#1F1F1F", linewidth = 0.35, width = 0.65) +
  labs(
    title = "Race Distribution Using Summarised Data",
    subtitle = "Using geom_col() with pre-counted values",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









This bar chart is created using geom_col(), which is suitable when the dataset has already been summarised. In this case, the table race_count contains the pre-calculated number of students in each race category, and the column n is mapped to the y-axis. Unlike geom_bar(), geom_col() does not perform automatic counting.

section: 2.3 Visualising the Distribution of English Scores
text:
2.3 Visualising the Distribution of English Scores
After examining the distribution of a categorical variable, the next step is to explore a numerical variable. In this section, the English scores are visualised to understand the overall score distribution, including the spread, concentration, and possible unusual values.

2.3.1 Dot Plot of English Scores
A dot plot gives a compact view of how individual English scores are distributed. Each dot represents observations around a score value, making it useful for seeing where the scores are clustered.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_dotplot(
    binwidth = 2.5,
    dotsize = 0.6,
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Dot Plot of English Scores",
    subtitle = "Each dot represents students grouped by similar score values",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )











2.3.2 Histogram of English Scores
The histogram shows the overall distribution of English scores more clearly than the dot plot. Most students are concentrated in the middle score ranges, while very low and very high scores appear less frequently.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#5B7F6E",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Histogram of English Scores",
    subtitle = "Distribution of English scores in 5-point intervals",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









English scores cluster mainly between 60 and 80, with the strongest concentration around the 70s. The thinner bars at both ends suggest that very low and near-perfect scores are relatively uncommon.


2.3.3 Modifying geom_histogram()
The appearance of a histogram can be adjusted by changing the arguments inside geom_histogram(). Here, the bin width is made wider so that the score distribution is grouped into broader intervals.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 10,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#A66A4C",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Distribution with Wider Bins",
    subtitle = "Using 10-point intervals",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









With wider bins, the histogram looks less detailed but shows the overall shape of the score distribution more clearly.


2.3.4 Modifying Aesthetic Mapping
Aesthetic mapping changes how variables are connected to visual features. In this histogram, GENDER is mapped to fill, so the bars show how English score distributions differ between male and female students.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Distribution by Gender",
    subtitle = "Using fill mapping inside aes()",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )









Mapping `GENDER` to `fill` adds a second layer of information to the histogram. The bars are now coloured by gender, making it easier to see how male and female students contribute to the overall English score distribution.


2.3.5 Density Plot of English Scores
A density plot provides a smoother view of the score distribution. It is useful when the goal is to see the general shape of the data without focusing on individual histogram bins.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_density(
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Density Plot of English Scores",
    subtitle = "A smoother view of the score distribution",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









The curve peaks around the higher-middle score range, which is consistent with the histogram pattern. Compared with the histogram, the density plot gives a cleaner view of the overall shape.


2.3.6 Boxplot of English Scores by Gender
A boxplot is useful for comparing the distribution of a numerical variable across groups. Here, English scores are compared between male and female students.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = GENDER, y = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.8,
    outlier.color = "#A66A4C",
    outlier.size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "English Scores by Gender",
    subtitle = "Comparing median, spread, and possible outliers",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "English Score",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









The boxplot makes the gender comparison more compact than the histogram. It highlights the median score, the spread of scores, and any possible outliers in each group.


2.3.7 Violin Plot of English Scores by Gender
Boxplots are compact, but they can feel a little too compressed. A violin plot opens up the shape of the distribution, making it easier to see where scores are packed more tightly.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = GENDER, y = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_violin(
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.75,
    trim = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    fill = "white",
    alpha = 0.7,
    outlier.color = "#A66A4C",
    outlier.size = 1.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Shape by Gender",
    subtitle = "Violin plot with a compact boxplot overlay",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "English Score",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









The violin shape makes the score pattern less flat than a boxplot. The wider sections mark where more students are clustered, while the narrow tails show thinner score ranges.


2.3.8 Scatter Plot of Maths and English Scores
A scatter plot is useful when the question shifts from “how one variable is distributed” to “how two variables move together”. Here, each point represents one student, with Maths score on the x-axis and English score on the y-axis.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Maths and English Scores",
    subtitle = "Each point represents one student",
    x = "Maths Score",
    y = "English Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









The point cloud leans clearly upward: stronger Maths scores usually come with stronger English scores. There are a few scattered exceptions, but the overall relationship is hard to miss.


2.3.9 Adding a Trend Line to the Scatter Plot
The scatter plot already hints at a positive relationship. Adding a smooth trend line makes that pattern easier to read, especially when there are many points on the chart.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.55,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "#A66A4C",
    fill = "#D8B8A2",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maths and English Scores with Trend Line",
    subtitle = "Linear trend added using geom_smooth()",
    x = "Maths Score",
    y = "English Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









The fitted line cuts cleanly through the point cloud, reinforcing the positive relationship between Maths and English scores. The shaded band gives a quick sense of uncertainty around the trend.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.4 Working with Statistical Summaries
So far, the charts have mostly shown raw observations. Statistical summaries go one level higher: instead of plotting every individual value, they calculate a summary value first, then display it.

2.4.1 Mean English Score by Gender


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = GENDER, y = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "bar",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.8,
    width = 0.6
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean English Score by Gender",
    subtitle = "Using stat_summary() to calculate group means",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Mean English Score",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









Instead of showing every English score, this chart compresses each gender group into one mean value. It is cleaner, but also more ruthless: the spread and outliers disappear, so the chart should be read together with the earlier boxplot.


2.4.2 Mean English Score with Error Bars
A mean bar alone looks clean, but it hides too much. Error bars add a quick check on how stable the mean comparison is.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = GENDER, y = ENGLISH, fill = GENDER)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "bar",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    alpha = 0.8,
    width = 0.6
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar",
    width = 0.18,
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean English Score by Gender with Error Bars",
    subtitle = "Bars show means; error bars show standard error",
    x = "Gender",
    y = "Mean English Score",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









The bars still show the average English score for each gender, but the error bars stop the chart from pretending the averages are perfectly fixed. It is a small addition, but it makes the comparison more honest.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.5 Faceting
Faceting splits one chart into smaller panels. Instead of squeezing every group into one plot, it gives each group its own little stage.

2.5.1 English Score Distribution by Class


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Distribution by Class",
    subtitle = "Each panel shows one class",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









Faceting makes class-level patterns easier to scan. Instead of mixing all students into one histogram, each class gets its own panel, so differences in spread and concentration are easier to spot.


2.5.2 Faceting by Gender and Race
facet_grid() arranges panels like a grid. This is useful when two categorical variables are involved and the comparison needs a cleaner structure.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#A66A4C",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  facet_grid(GENDER ~ RACE) +
  labs(
    title = "English Score Distribution by Gender and Race",
    subtitle = "Rows show gender; columns show race",
    x = "English Score",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









The grid layout is stricter than facet_wrap(): gender runs down the rows, while race runs across the columns. Some panels are sparse, which is a useful reminder that subgroup comparisons can get fragile when the sample size becomes small.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.6 Coordinates
Coordinate settings change how a plot is displayed without changing the underlying data. A simple example is flipping the x-axis and y-axis to make a bar chart easier to read.

2.6.1 Flipping the Bar Chart


Code
ggplot(data = race_count,
       aes(x = RACE, y = n)) +
  geom_col(
    fill = "#2A6F6F",
    color = "#1F1F1F",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Race Distribution with Flipped Coordinates",
    subtitle = "Same data, different reading direction",
    x = "Race",
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









Flipping the chart does not change the counts. It simply turns the bars sideways, which makes category labels easier to read and gives the chart a cleaner rhythm.


2.6.2 Zooming into the Score Range
Sometimes the full axis range is not the most useful view. Here, the plot is zoomed into the main score range so the dense middle section is easier to inspect.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(40, 100),
    ylim = c(40, 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Zoomed View of Maths and English Scores",
    subtitle = "Using coord_cartesian() to focus on the main score range",
    x = "Maths Score",
    y = "English Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )









This zoomed view keeps the original data intact but focuses the display on the main score band. It is cleaner for reading the dense area, without pretending the lower scores never existed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.7 Working with Themes
Themes control the non-data parts of a chart: background, grid lines, title style, axis text, legend position, and spacing. A good theme should not fight for attention; it should make the data easier to read.

2.7.1 Applying a Custom Theme


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    color = "#A66A4C",
    fill = "#D8B8A2",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maths and English Scores with a Custom Theme",
    subtitle = "Theme settings improve readability without changing the data",
    x = "Maths Score",
    y = "English Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.25, color = "grey85")
  )









The theme changes do not alter the data or the statistical relationship. They simply clean up the visual surface: less noise, clearer text, and a chart that feels more intentional.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: A Layered Grammar of Graphics and Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
2.8 Summary
This exercise shows how ggplot2 builds charts layer by layer. The same dataset can be explored from different angles: categorical distributions with bar charts, score distributions with dot plots, histograms and density plots, group comparisons with boxplots and violin plots, and score relationships with scatter plots.
The main takeaway is that ggplot2 is not just about drawing charts. It is about deciding what each layer does: what data to use, what variables to map, what geometric object to choose, what statistical summary to calculate, how to split panels with facets, how to adjust coordinates, and how to refine the final look with themes.

title: Hands-on_Ex06c
text:
A heatmap is used to visualise values in a table through colour. It is especially useful when a dataset contains many observations and several numerical variables. Instead of reading values one by one, a heatmap allows us to detect high-value and low-value patterns quickly.
In this hands-on exercise, we use the World Happiness 2018 dataset to create static and interactive heatmaps. The main analytical goal is to compare countries across different happiness-related indicators, including happiness score, GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity and perceptions of corruption.
By the end of this exercise, we should be able to:

import and prepare the World Happiness 2018 dataset;
select suitable numerical variables for heatmap analysis;
transform a data frame into a matrix;
create static heatmaps using base R;
create interactive heatmaps using heatmaply;
compare scaling, normalising and percentising methods;
apply clustering and seriation methods;
improve the heatmap with a customised colour palette.




The packages used in this exercise are tidyverse, heatmaply, seriation, dendextend and knitr.

pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  heatmaply,
  seriation,
  dendextend,
  knitr
)


The downloaded binary packages are in
    /var/folders/54/lskjc21j5kngz8h14l28h44c0000gn/T//RtmpY0a9GC/downloaded_packages





The dataset used in this exercise is WHData-2018.csv. It contains the 2018 World Happiness data by country. The variables include happiness score and several explanatory indicators.
The important columns used in this exercise are:

Country
Region

GDP per capita

)

}

Now each row represents a country and each column represents a happiness-related indicator.



To avoid package-version issues, the following helper functions are created manually.

normalise_matrix <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 2, function(col) {
    (col - min(col, na.rm = TRUE)) / 
      (max(col, na.rm = TRUE) - min(col, na.rm = TRUE))
  })
}

scale_matrix <- function(x) {
  scale(x)
}

percentise_matrix <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 2, function(col) {
    rank(col, ties.method = "average", na.last = "keep") / 
      sum(!is.na(col))
  })
}

These functions will be used later to compare different transformation methods.




Static heatmaps are useful for a quick overview. We begin with the base R heatmap() function.


The first heatmap keeps the original row and column order.

The plotThe code chunk



heatmap(
  wh_matrix,
  Rowv = NA,
  Colv = NA,
  scale = "none",
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  margins = c(10, 4),
  cexRow = 0.45,
  cexCol = 0.8
)











heatmap(
  wh_matrix,
  Rowv = NA,
  Colv = NA,
  scale = "none",
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  margins = c(10, 4),
  cexRow = 0.45,
  cexCol = 0.8
)




This first version is useful as a basic check. However, the variables are measured on different scales, so direct comparison is not ideal.



Column scaling makes each indicator comparable by standardising values within each column.

The plotThe code chunk



heatmap(
  wh_matrix,
  scale = "column",
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  margins = c(10, 4),
  cexRow = 0.45,
  cexCol = 0.8
)











heatmap(
  wh_matrix,
  scale = "column",
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  margins = c(10, 4),
  cexRow = 0.45,
  cexCol = 0.8
)




This version is more meaningful because each colour shows whether a country is relatively high or low within a specific indicator.






Note



For this dataset, scaling is important because happiness score, GDP per capita and corruption perception are not measured on the same numerical scale.






Interactive heatmaps allow users to hover over cells and inspect values directly.



The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_matrix,
  main = "Interactive Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators, 2018",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








heatmaply(
  wh_matrix,
  main = "Interactive Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators, 2018",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




This chart allows the viewer to explore country-level indicator values interactively.




Different transformation methods can change the interpretation of a heatmap. In this section, we compare scaling, normalising and percentising.


Scaling converts each variable into standard deviation units.

wh_scaled <- scale_matrix(wh_matrix)


The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_scaled,
  main = "Scaled Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








wh_scaled <- scale_matrix(wh_matrix)

heatmaply(
  wh_scaled,
  main = "Scaled Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




Scaling is useful when the objective is to compare whether a country is above or below average for each indicator.



Normalising converts each variable into a 0 to 1 range.

wh_normalised <- normalise_matrix(wh_matrix)


The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  main = "Normalised Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








wh_normalised <- normalise_matrix(wh_matrix)

heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  main = "Normalised Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




Normalising is useful when we want all indicators to be placed on the same 0 to 1 scale.



Percentising converts values into percentile-style ranks.

wh_percentised <- percentise_matrix(wh_matrix)


The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_percentised,
  main = "Percentised Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








wh_percentised <- percentise_matrix(wh_matrix)

heatmaply(
  wh_percentised,
  main = "Percentised Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




Percentising is useful when the focus is on relative ranking rather than raw numerical distance.




Heatmaps are often combined with clustering to group similar observations together.


The distance matrix is calculated from the normalised data.

wh_dist <- dist(
  wh_normalised,
  method = "euclidean"
)





wh_hclust <- hclust(
  wh_dist,
  method = "average"
)


plot(
  wh_hclust,
  labels = FALSE,
  main = "Hierarchical Clustering of Countries",
  xlab = "Countries",
  sub = ""
)








The dendrogram shows how countries are grouped based on similarity across selected happiness indicators.




The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  dist_method = "euclidean",
  hclust_method = "average",
  k_row = 4,
  main = "Normalised Heatmap with Four Country Clusters",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  dist_method = "euclidean",
  hclust_method = "average",
  k_row = 4,
  main = "Normalised Heatmap with Four Country Clusters",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




This version groups countries with similar happiness indicator profiles.




Seriation improves the ordering of rows and columns in a heatmap. A better ordering can make visual patterns easier to detect.



The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  seriate = "OLO",
  main = "Heatmap with Optimal Leaf Ordering",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  seriate = "OLO",
  main = "Heatmap with Optimal Leaf Ordering",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




Optimal Leaf Ordering helps place similar countries closer together while preserving the hierarchical clustering structure.




The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  seriate = "mean",
  main = "Heatmap with Mean Ordering",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  seriate = "mean",
  main = "Heatmap with Mean Ordering",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




Mean ordering provides a simpler arrangement based on average values.




The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  seriate = "none",
  main = "Heatmap without Additional Seriation",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  seriate = "none",
  main = "Heatmap without Additional Seriation",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




This version keeps the ordering simpler and avoids additional row rotation.




Colour design is important because heatmaps rely heavily on colour interpretation.

my_teal_palette <- colorRampPalette(
  c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F")
)(256)

my_diverging_palette <- colorRampPalette(
  c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F")
)(256)




The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  seriate = "none",
  colors = my_teal_palette,
  main = "Normalised Heatmap with Custom Teal Palette",
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  seriate = "none",
  colors = my_teal_palette,
  main = "Normalised Heatmap with Custom Teal Palette",
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




The custom teal palette keeps low values light and high values dark.




The final version combines normalised values, custom colour design, row clustering and readable labels.

The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  Colv = NA,
  seriate = "none",
  colors = my_teal_palette,
  k_row = 5,
  margins = c(NA, 200, 60, NA),
  fontsize_row = 4,
  fontsize_col = 9,
  main = "World Happiness Score and Indicators by Country, 2018",
  xlab = "World Happiness Indicators",
  ylab = "Countries"
)








heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  Colv = NA,
  seriate = "none",
  colors = my_teal_palette,
  k_row = 5,
  margins = c(NA, 200, 60, NA),
  fontsize_row = 4,
  fontsize_col = 9,
  main = "World Happiness Score and Indicators by Country, 2018",
  xlab = "World Happiness Indicators",
  ylab = "Countries"

To avoid package-version issues, the following helper functions are created manually.

normalise_matrix <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 2, function(col) {
    (col - min(col, na.rm = TRUE)) / 
      (max(col, na.rm = TRUE) - min(col, na.rm = TRUE))
  })
}

scale_matrix <- function(x) {
  scale(x)
}

percentise_matrix <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 2, function(col) {
    rank(col, ties.method = "average", na.last = "keep") / 
      sum(!is.na(col))
  })
}

These functions will be used later to compare different transformation methods.

text:
Static heatmaps are useful for a quick overview. We begin with the base R heatmap() function.


The first heatmap keeps the original row and column order.

The plotThe code chunk



heatmap(
  wh_matrix,
  Rowv = NA,
  Colv = NA,
  scale = "none",
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  margins = c(10, 4),
  cexRow = 0.45,
  cexCol = 0.8
)











heatmap(
  wh_matrix,
  Rowv = NA,
  Colv = NA,
  scale = "none",
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  margins = c(10, 4),
  cexRow = 0.45,
  cexCol = 0.8
)




This first version is useful as a basic check. However, the variables are measured on different scales, so direct comparison is not ideal.



Column scaling makes each indicator comparable by standardising values within each column.

The plotThe code chunk



heatmap(
  wh_matrix,
  scale = "column",
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  margins = c(10, 4),
  cexRow = 0.45,
  cexCol = 0.8
)











heatmap(
  wh_matrix,
  scale = "column",
  col = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  margins = c(10, 4),
  cexRow = 0.45,
  cexCol = 0.8
)




This version is more meaningful because each colour shows whether a country is relatively high or low within a specific indicator.






Note



For this dataset, scaling is important because happiness score, GDP per capita and corruption perception are not measured on the same numerical scale.

title: Hands-on_Ex06c
text:
Different transformation methods can change the interpretation of a heatmap. In this section, we compare scaling, normalising and percentising.


Scaling converts each variable into standard deviation units.

wh_scaled <- scale_matrix(wh_matrix)


The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_scaled,
  main = "Scaled Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)








wh_scaled <- scale_matrix(wh_matrix)

heatmaply(
  wh_scaled,
  main = "Scaled Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)




Scaling is useful when the objective is to compare whether a country is above or below average for each indicator.



Normalising converts each variable into a 0 to 1 range.

wh_normalised <- normalise_matrix(wh_matrix)


The plotThe code chunk



heatmaply(
  wh_normalised,
  main = "Normalised Heatmap of World Happiness Indicators",
  colors = colorRampPalette(c("#F7FBFF", "#A8DADC", "#2A6F6F"))(256),
  fontsize_row = 5,
  fontsize_col = 9
)
