The variable rate represents the cumulative fatality rate. The variable rate.se represents the standard error of the fatality rate.
A smaller standard error means the rate estimate is more stable. A larger standard error means the rate estimate is more uncertain.
Next, the weighted mean fatality rate is calculated. The weighting gives more influence to observations with smaller standard errors.

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1 / df$rate.se^2)

fit.mean

[1] 0.01496959





To draw the funnel shape, we calculate control limits across the range of positive case counts.
The 95% limits use 1.96, while the 99.9% limits use 3.29.

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)

number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean * (1 - fit.mean)) / number.seq)
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean * (1 - fit.mean)) / number.seq)

number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean * (1 - fit.mean)) / number.seq)
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean * (1 - fit.mean)) / number.seq)

This chart should not be read like a normal scatterplot. The main question is not simply which sub-district has the highest fatality rate. The better question is whether the fatality rate is unusually high or low after considering the number of positive cases.
Points inside the funnel are generally within the expected range of variation. Points outside the outer limit deserve closer investigation.

The interactive version is useful when there are many sub-districts. Instead of labelling every point and making the plot messy, we can keep the visual clean and use hover text for detail.

As a small extension, we can classify each sub-district based on whether it falls above, below or inside the 99.9% control limits.
This makes the funnel plot more actionable because it turns the visual result into a simple table for follow-up analysis.

  mutate(

      rate > ul999_actual ~ "Above 99.9% limit",
      rate < ll999_actual ~ "Below 99.9% limit",

title: Hands-on_Ex05b
text:
In this hands-on exercise, we focus on visual statistical analysis. Instead of producing charts that only show patterns, we will use statistical visualisation to combine graphics with test results.
The main package used in this exercise is ggstatsplot. It extends ggplot2 by adding statistical test results directly into the visual output. This is useful because the viewer can see both the chart and the statistical evidence in one place.
By the end of this exercise, we should be able to:

use ggstatsplot to create graphics with statistical information;
conduct a one-sample test using gghistostats();
explain the basic idea of Bayes Factor;
compare two groups using ggbetweenstats();
compare more than two groups using one-way ANOVA;
test correlation using ggscatterstats();
test association between categorical variables using ggbarstats().




ggstatsplot is an extension of ggplot2. The main idea is simple: instead of separating the chart and the statistical test output, ggstatsplot puts them together.
This is helpful for visual analytics because the chart does not only show the shape of the data. It also provides statistical information such as sample size, p-value, test statistic, confidence interval and Bayes Factor.
In normal data analysis, we may first draw a plot and then run a separate statistical test. With ggstatsplot, these two steps can be combined into one visual output. This makes the result easier to read, especially when the audience needs both visual and statistical interpretation.





In this exercise, ggstatsplot and tidyverse will be used. tidyverse is mainly used for importing and preparing data, while ggstatsplot is used to create the statistical graphics.

pacman::p_load(ggstatsplot, tidyverse, ggthemes)

also installing the dependencies 'fracdiff', 'lmtest', 'timeDate', 'urca', 'zoo', 'RcppArmadillo', 'rbibutils', 'cowplot', 'Deriv', 'forecast', 'microbenchmark', 'SparseM', 'Rdpack', 'minqa', 'nloptr', 'doBy', 'carData', 'abind', 'Formula', 'quantreg', 'elliptic', 'contfrac', 'deSolve', 'plyr', 'lme4', 'pbkrtest', 'lmerTest', 'car', 'reformulas', 'coda', 'pbapply', 'mvtnorm', 'MatrixModels', 'hypergeo', 'RcppEigen', 'multcompView', 'gmp', 'Rmpfr', 'SuppDists', 'kSamples', 'BWStest', 'desc', 'RcppParallel', 'reshape', 'bayestestR', 'reshape2', 'prismatic', 'afex', 'BayesFactor', 'effectsize', 'PMCMRplus', 'rstantools', 'WRS2', 'correlation', 'datawizard', 'ggcorrplot', 'ggside', 'ggsignif', 'insight', 'paletteer', 'parameters', 'performance', 'statsExpressions'



The downloaded binary packages are in
    /var/folders/54/lskjc21j5kngz8h14l28h44c0000gn/T//RtmpmsLkFy/downloaded_packages

The dataset used in this exercise is Exam_data.csv. It contains student examination records, including English, Maths and Science scores, together with grouping variables such as class, gender and race.

The key numeric variables in this dataset are ENGLISH, MATHS and SCIENCE. These variables can be used for statistical comparison, correlation analysis and distribution-based testing.




A one-sample test is used when we want to compare one numeric variable against a fixed reference value. In this example, we test whether the English scores are meaningfully different from a reference score of 60.
The function gghistostats() creates a histogram and adds statistical test results directly to the plot.

The plotThe code chunk



set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores",
  title = "One-sample Test of English Scores",
  subtitle = "Testing whether English scores differ from the reference value of 60",
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)











set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores",
  title = "One-sample Test of English Scores",
  subtitle = "Testing whether English scores differ from the reference value of 60",
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)




The histogram shows the distribution of English scores, while the statistical annotation gives the test result. This is more useful than a normal histogram because it connects the visual pattern with statistical evidence.
In this case, the reference value is set as 60. If the centre of the distribution is clearly above or below 60, the visual result and the statistical test should point in the same direction.



Bayes Factor is used to compare the strength of evidence between two competing hypotheses.
In a simple setting:

H0 means the null hypothesis;
H1 means the alternative hypothesis;
BF10 compares how much more likely the data is under H1 than under H0.

If BF10 is large, the data provides stronger evidence for the alternative hypothesis. If BF10 is close to 1, the evidence is weak or inconclusive. If BF10 is very small, the evidence may support the null hypothesis instead.
A simple way to understand it:

bayes_factor_example <- tibble(
  BF10 = c(1, 3, 10, 30, 100),
  Interpretation = c(
    "No clear evidence",
    "Anecdotal evidence for H1",
    "Moderate evidence for H1",
    "Strong evidence for H1",
    "Extreme evidence for H1"
  )
)

bayes_factor_example

# A tibble: 5 × 2
   BF10 Interpretation           
  <dbl> <chr>                    
1     1 No clear evidence        
2     3 Anecdotal evidence for H1
3    10 Moderate evidence for H1 
4    30 Strong evidence for H1   
5   100 Extreme evidence for H1  


Bayes Factor is useful because it does not only ask whether a result is statistically significant. It asks how strong the evidence is for one hypothesis compared with another.



The interpretation of Bayes Factor should not be treated mechanically, but the following table gives a common practical guide.

bf_interpretation <- tibble(
  Bayes_Factor = c("1 to 3", "3 to 10", "10 to 30", "30 to 100", "> 100"),
  Evidence = c(
    "Weak evidence",
    "Moderate evidence",
    "Strong evidence",
    "Very strong evidence",
    "Extreme evidence"
  )
)

bf_interpretation

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  Bayes_Factor Evidence            
  <chr>        <chr>               
1 1 to 3       Weak evidence       
2 3 to 10      Moderate evidence   
3 10 to 30     Strong evidence     
4 30 to 100    Very strong evidence
5 > 100        Extreme evidence    


The main idea is that Bayes Factor gives a graded interpretation. This is different from a p-value, where the result is often simplified into significant or not significant.






Note



A p-value and a Bayes Factor answer different questions. A p-value focuses on the probability of observing the data under the null hypothesis, while a Bayes Factor compares the relative evidence between two hypotheses.





A two-sample test is used when we want to compare a numeric variable between two groups. In this example, Maths scores are compared by gender.
The function ggbetweenstats() automatically creates a comparison plot and adds statistical test results.

The plotThe code chunk



ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = GENDER,
  y = MATHS,
  type = "np",
  title = "Maths Scores by Gender",
  subtitle = "Two-group comparison using a non-parametric test",
  xlab = "Gender",
  ylab = "Maths scores",
  messages = FALSE,
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)











ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = GENDER,
  y = MATHS,
  type = "np",
  title = "Maths Scores by Gender",
  subtitle = "Two-group comparison using a non-parametric test",
  xlab = "Gender",
  ylab = "Maths scores",
  messages = FALSE,
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)




The argument type = "np" means that a non-parametric test is used. This is useful when we do not want to assume that the scores are normally distributed.
This chart allows us to compare the distribution, median and statistical difference between male and female students in Maths performance.



When there are more than two groups, a one-way ANOVA can be used to test whether the mean values differ across groups. In this example, English scores are compared across different race groups.
Here, ggbetweenstats() is used again, but this time the grouping variable has more than two categories.

The plotThe code chunk



ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = RACE,
  y = ENGLISH,
  type = "p",
  mean.ci = TRUE,
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  title = "English Scores by Race",
  subtitle = "One-way ANOVA with pairwise comparisons",
  xlab = "Race",
  ylab = "English scores",
  messages = FALSE,
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)











ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = RACE,
  y = ENGLISH,
  type = "p",
  mean.ci = TRUE,
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  title = "English Scores by Race",
  subtitle = "One-way ANOVA with pairwise comparisons",
  xlab = "Race",
  ylab = "English scores",
  messages = FALSE,
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)




The argument type = "p" means a parametric test is used. The argument mean.ci = TRUE adds the confidence interval around the mean.
The pairwise comparison settings help us identify which group differences are statistically meaningful.
The argument pairwise.display = "s" means that only significant pairwise comparisons will be displayed. This keeps the plot cleaner and avoids too much unnecessary annotation.






Tip



For pairwise.display, "s" shows only significant comparisons, "ns" shows only non-significant comparisons, and "all" shows all pairwise comparisons.




To support the visual result, we can also create a simple summary table by race. This does not replace the ANOVA test, but it helps us understand the group-level pattern more clearly.

race_english_summary <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_english = mean(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_english = median(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),

Correlation analysis is used to examine whether two numeric variables move together. In this example, we test the relationship between Maths scores and English scores.
The function ggscatterstats() creates a scatterplot and adds correlation test results.

title: Hands-on_Ex05b
Hands-on_Ex05b
text:
ggstatsplot is an extension of ggplot2. The main idea is simple: instead of separating the chart and the statistical test output, ggstatsplot puts them together.
This is helpful for visual analytics because the chart does not only show the shape of the data. It also provides statistical information such as sample size, p-value, test statistic, confidence interval and Bayes Factor.
In normal data analysis, we may first draw a plot and then run a separate statistical test. With ggstatsplot, these two steps can be combined into one visual output. This makes the result easier to read, especially when the audience needs both visual and statistical interpretation.

title: Hands-on_Ex05b
text:
A one-sample test is used when we want to compare one numeric variable against a fixed reference value. In this example, we test whether the English scores are meaningfully different from a reference score of 60.
The function gghistostats() creates a histogram and adds statistical test results directly to the plot.

The plotThe code chunk



set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores",
  title = "One-sample Test of English Scores",
  subtitle = "Testing whether English scores differ from the reference value of 60",
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)











set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores",
  title = "One-sample Test of English Scores",
  subtitle = "Testing whether English scores differ from the reference value of 60",
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)




The histogram shows the distribution of English scores, while the statistical annotation gives the test result. This is more useful than a normal histogram because it connects the visual pattern with statistical evidence.
In this case, the reference value is set as 60. If the centre of the distribution is clearly above or below 60, the visual result and the statistical test should point in the same direction.

title: Hands-on_Ex05b
text:
Bayes Factor is used to compare the strength of evidence between two competing hypotheses.
In a simple setting:

H0 means the null hypothesis;
H1 means the alternative hypothesis;
BF10 compares how much more likely the data is under H1 than under H0.

If BF10 is large, the data provides stronger evidence for the alternative hypothesis. If BF10 is close to 1, the evidence is weak or inconclusive. If BF10 is very small, the evidence may support the null hypothesis instead.
A simple way to understand it:

bayes_factor_example <- tibble(
  BF10 = c(1, 3, 10, 30, 100),
  Interpretation = c(
    "No clear evidence",
    "Anecdotal evidence for H1",
    "Moderate evidence for H1",
    "Strong evidence for H1",
    "Extreme evidence for H1"
  )
)

bayes_factor_example

# A tibble: 5 × 2
   BF10 Interpretation           
  <dbl> <chr>                    
1     1 No clear evidence        
2     3 Anecdotal evidence for H1
3    10 Moderate evidence for H1 
4    30 Strong evidence for H1   
5   100 Extreme evidence for H1  


Bayes Factor is useful because it does not only ask whether a result is statistically significant. It asks how strong the evidence is for one hypothesis compared with another.

title: Hands-on_Ex05b
text:
The interpretation of Bayes Factor should not be treated mechanically, but the following table gives a common practical guide.

bf_interpretation <- tibble(
  Bayes_Factor = c("1 to 3", "3 to 10", "10 to 30", "30 to 100", "> 100"),
  Evidence = c(
    "Weak evidence",
    "Moderate evidence",
    "Strong evidence",
    "Very strong evidence",
    "Extreme evidence"
  )
)

5 > 100        Extreme evidence    


The main idea is that Bayes Factor gives a graded interpretation. This is different from a p-value, where the result is often simplified into significant or not significant.






Note



A p-value and a Bayes Factor answer different questions. A p-value focuses on the probability of observing the data under the null hypothesis, while a Bayes Factor compares the relative evidence between two hypotheses.

When there are more than two groups, a one-way ANOVA can be used to test whether the mean values differ across groups. In this example, English scores are compared across different race groups.

)











ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = RACE,
  y = ENGLISH,
  type = "p",
  mean.ci = TRUE,
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  title = "English Scores by Race",
  subtitle = "One-way ANOVA with pairwise comparisons",

  ylab = "English scores",
  messages = FALSE,
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)




The argument type = "p" means a parametric test is used. The argument mean.ci = TRUE adds the confidence interval around the mean.
The pairwise comparison settings help us identify which group differences are statistically meaningful.
The argument pairwise.display = "s" means that only significant pairwise comparisons will be displayed. This keeps the plot cleaner and avoids too much unnecessary annotation.






Tip



For pairwise.display, "s" shows only significant comparisons, "ns" shows only non-significant comparisons, and "all" shows all pairwise comparisons.




To support the visual result, we can also create a simple summary table by race. This does not replace the ANOVA test, but it helps us understand the group-level pattern more clearly.

race_english_summary <- exam %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_english = mean(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_english = median(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_english = sd(ENGLISH, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_english))

title: Hands-on_Ex05b
text:
Correlation analysis is used to examine whether two numeric variables move together. In this example, we test the relationship between Maths scores and English scores.
The function ggscatterstats() creates a scatterplot and adds correlation test results.

The plotThe code chunk



ggscatterstats(
  data = exam,
  x = MATHS,
  y = ENGLISH,
  marginal = FALSE,
  title = "Relationship between Maths and English Scores",
  xlab = "Maths scores",
  ylab = "English scores",
  messages = FALSE,
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)











ggscatterstats(

  x = MATHS,

  xlab = "Maths scores",
  ylab = "English scores",
  messages = FALSE,
  ggtheme = ggplot2::theme_minimal()
)




The scatterplot shows whether students with higher Maths scores also tend to have higher English scores. The statistical annotation helps us judge whether the relationship is meaningful or weak.
If the points move upward from left to right, the relationship is positive. If the points are widely scattered with no clear direction, the relationship is weak.


To add a small extension, we can calculate the correlation between the three exam subjects: English, Maths and Science.
This gives a quick numerical overview before looking at more detailed statistical plots.

title: Visual Multivariate Analysis with Parallel Coordinates Plot
text:
4 Static parallel coordinates plot

4.1 Simple parallel coordinates plot
The first plot uses only the selected numerical variables from the dataset. In this example, columns 7 to 12 are used because they contain the main World Happiness indicators.

ggparcoord(
  data = wh,
  columns = c(7:12)
)








This basic version is technically correct, but it is difficult to interpret because all lines use the same visual treatment and the variables are not yet grouped by region.


4.2 Parallel coordinates plot with grouping, scaling and boxplot
The next version improves the plot by adding several important arguments.

ggparcoord(
  data = wh,
  columns = c(7:12),
  groupColumn = 2,
  scale = "uniminmax",
  alphaLines = 0.25,
  boxplot = TRUE,
  title = "Parallel Coordinates Plot of World Happiness Indicators"
)








Important arguments used above:

groupColumn = 2 colours the lines by the second column, which is the geographical region.
scale = "uniminmax" rescales each variable from 0 to 1, so variables with different units can be compared on the same plot.
alphaLines = 0.25 makes the lines more transparent, reducing visual clutter.
boxplot = TRUE adds a boxplot summary for each variable.
title adds a clear chart title.

This version is more useful because it allows regional patterns to appear more clearly.


4.3 Parallel coordinates plot with facets
Because the plot contains many regions, a single chart can still be visually crowded. Faceting splits the chart into smaller panels by region.

ggparcoord(
  data = wh,
  columns = c(7:12),
  groupColumn = 2,
  scale = "uniminmax",
  alphaLines = 0.25,
  boxplot = TRUE,
  title = "World Happiness Indicators by Region"
) +
  facet_wrap(~ Region)








The faceted version makes it easier to compare patterns within each region separately. However, some x-axis labels may overlap because the variable names are long.


4.4 Rotating x-axis labels
To improve readability, the x-axis labels can be rotated using theme().

ggparcoord(
  data = wh,
  columns = c(7:12),
  groupColumn = 2,
  scale = "uniminmax",
  alphaLines = 0.25,
  boxplot = TRUE,
  title = "World Happiness Indicators by Region"
) +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30)
  )








Rotating the labels helps, but the text position is still not ideal because the labels can be too close to the plot area.


4.5 Adjusting rotated x-axis labels
The final static version adjusts the horizontal justification of the rotated labels.

ggparcoord(
  data = wh,
  columns = c(7:12),
  groupColumn = 2,
  scale = "uniminmax",
  alphaLines = 0.25,
  boxplot = TRUE,
  title = "World Happiness Indicators by Region"
) +
  facet_wrap(~ Region) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )








This is the cleanest static version because it combines grouping, scaling, transparency, boxplots, faceting, and readable axis labels.

5 Interactive parallel coordinates plot
The parallelPlot package can be used to create an interactive parallel coordinates plot. This is useful because the viewer can explore variables more flexibly.
Before plotting, a smaller data frame is created by selecting the happiness score and the main numerical indicators.

wh_interactive <- wh %>%
  select(
    "Happiness score",
    c(7:12)
  )

glimpse(wh_interactive)

$ `Perceptions of corruption`    <dbl> 0.032, 0.000, 0.009, 0.039, 0.034, 0.17…



5.1 Basic interactive plot

parallelPlot(
  wh_interactive,
  width = 800,
  height = 450
)





The basic interactive chart allows the user to explore the relationship between the happiness score and the selected indicators.


5.2 Rotating axis titles
Some variable names are long. rotateTitle = TRUE rotates the axis titles and makes the chart easier to read.

parallelPlot(
  wh_interactive,
  rotateTitle = TRUE,
  width = 800,
  height = 450
)







5.3 Changing the continuous colour scheme
The colour scheme can be changed using the continuousCS argument.

parallelPlot(
  wh_interactive,
  rotateTitle = TRUE,
  continuousCS = "YlOrRd",
  width = 800,
  height = 450
)





This version uses a yellow-orange-red colour scheme, which helps show value intensity more clearly when an axis is selected.


5.4 Adding histograms to the axes
Histograms can be displayed along the axes by using the histoVisibility argument.

histoVisibility <- rep(TRUE, ncol(wh_interactive))

parallelPlot(
  wh_interactive,
  rotateTitle = TRUE,
  histoVisibility = histoVisibility,
  width = 800,
  height = 450
)





The histogram view gives extra distribution information for each variable, so the chart is not only showing multivariate patterns but also the shape of each variable’s distribution.

title: Hands-on_Ex06a
text:
A ternary plot is used to visualise data made up of three parts. The three components are placed inside a triangle, and each point represents how the total is divided among the three components.
This type of chart is useful when the main question is not about absolute size, but about composition. For example, a population area can be described by the proportion of young residents, economically active residents and old residents.
In this hands-on exercise, ternary plots are used to study the population structure of Singapore. The focus is on comparing the balance between three age groups across planning areas and subzones.
By the end of this exercise, we should be able to:

prepare population data for ternary plotting;
derive young, active and old population measures;
create a static ternary plot using ggtern;
improve the ternary plot with labels, colour and theme settings;
create an interactive ternary plot using plotly;
interpret population structure from a compositional point of view.




For this exercise, three main groups of packages are required.
ggtern is used to create static ternary diagrams. plotly is used to build interactive ternary plots. tidyverse is used for importing, cleaning and reshaping the data.

pacman::p_load(plotly, ggtern, tidyverse, knitr)

also installing the dependencies 'DEoptimR', 'tensorA', 'robustbase', 'bayesm', 'compositions', 'latex2exp', 'proto', 'hexbin'



The downloaded binary packages are in
    /var/folders/54/lskjc21j5kngz8h14l28h44c0000gn/T//RtmpHMd3iN/downloaded_packages



ggtern installed







The dataset used in this hands-on exercise is respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv. It contains Singapore resident population data by planning area, subzone, age group, sex and dwelling type.
For this exercise, the key variables are:

Year: the year of observation;
PA: planning area;
SZ: subzone;
AG: age group;
Population: number of residents.

The goal is to aggregate age groups into three broad categories:

YOUNG: younger population;
ACTIVE: economically active age group;
OLD: older population.




To reduce path errors during rendering, the code below checks several possible file locations. This is useful because your data file may be stored inside the current exercise folder or inside the common data folder.

pop_path <- case_when(
  file.exists("respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv") ~ "respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv",
  file.exists("data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv") ~ "data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv",
  file.exists("../data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv") ~ "../data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv",
  file.exists("../../data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv") ~ "../../data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv",
  TRUE ~ NA_character_
)

if (is.na(pop_path)) {

}

The imported dataset is in tidy format, meaning each row represents a specific combination of year, area, subzone, age group and other demographic attributes.



Before building the ternary plot, the data must be reshaped. Each age group is originally stored as a category under AG. To calculate broad age groups, we first spread the age groups into separate columns.
The three derived measures are:

YOUNG: sum of younger age groups;
ACTIVE: sum of working-age groups;
OLD: sum of older age groups.


agpop_mutated <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(`Year` = as.character(Year)) %>%
  spread(AG, Population) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8], na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16], na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21], na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24], na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(Year == 2018) %>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)

This extension makes the interpretation more direct. Instead of only saying that an area has many young or old residents, we can describe its population structure as a proportion of the total population.




A ternary plot places three variables on a triangular coordinate system. Every point is positioned according to the balance of the three components.
For this exercise:

the bottom-left axis represents young population;
the bottom-right axis represents active population;
the top axis represents old population.

A point closer to one corner means that the corresponding component has a higher share.


The simplest ternary plot can be created using ggtern(). In the code below, YOUNG, ACTIVE and OLD are mapped to the three ternary axes.

The plotThe code chunk



ggtern(
  data = agpop_mutated,
  aes(x = YOUNG,
      y = ACTIVE,
      z = OLD)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 1.6
  )











ggtern(
  data = agpop_mutated,
  aes(x = YOUNG,
      y = ACTIVE,
      z = OLD)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 1.6
  )




This first plot is useful as a basic check. It confirms whether the three age groups can be displayed in a ternary coordinate system.
However, the chart still needs better labels and styling before it becomes suitable for interpretation.



The next version adds a clear title and applies a cleaner ternary theme. A muted teal colour is used to keep the visual style consistent with the previous exercises.

The plotThe code chunk



ggtern(
  data = agpop_mutated,
  aes(x = YOUNG,
      y = ACTIVE,
      z = OLD)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 1.7
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population Structure of Singapore, 2018",
    subtitle = "Ternary plot of young, active and old population groups",
    T = "Young",
    L = "Active",
    R = "Old"
  ) +
  theme_rgbw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

This plot shows how Singapore’s subzones differ in population composition. Areas with a relatively older population will move closer to the old corner, while areas with more working-age residents will be located closer to the active side.



A useful extension is to map total population to point size. This allows the plot to show both composition and relative scale.
The triangle still shows the age structure, while the point size gives a quick sense of which subzones have larger population bases.

The plotThe code chunk

  data = agpop_share,

  scale_size_continuous(
    name = "Total population",

  ) +
  labs(

  theme_rgbw() +

This version is slightly more informative because it avoids treating every subzone as equally large. A small subzone and a large subzone may have similar composition, but they matter differently when interpreted from a planning perspective.



To add more analytical value, we can classify subzones by whether their old population share is above the median. This does not overcomplicate the analysis, but it makes the ternary plot easier to interpret.

The interactive ternary plot is created using plot_ly(). This allows the user to hover over each point and inspect the area name, subzone, total population and age-group shares.


The helper functions below are used to format the plot annotation and ternary axes.

label <- function(txt) {
  list(
    text = txt,
    x = 0.1,
    y = 1,
    ax = 0,
    ay = 0,
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    align = "center",
    font = list(
      family = "serif",
      size = 15,
      color = "white"
    ),
    bgcolor = "#2A6F6F",
    bordercolor = "#1F1F1F",
    borderwidth = 2
  )
}

axis <- function(txt) {
  list(
    title = txt,
    tickformat = ".0%",
    tickfont = list(size = 10)
  )
}

ternaryAxes <- list(
  aaxis = axis("Young"),
  baxis = axis("Active"),
  caxis = axis("Old")
)





The plotThe code chunk



plot_ly(
  agpop_share,
  a = ~YOUNG_SHARE,
  b = ~ACTIVE_SHARE,
  c = ~OLD_SHARE,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  color = ~Ageing_Group,
  colors = c("#2A6F6F", "#D95F02"),
  marker = list(
    size = 7,
    opacity = 0.75,
    line = list(
      color = "#1F1F1F",
      width = 0.5
    )
  ),
  text = ~paste(
    "Planning Area:", PA,
    "<br>Subzone:", SZ,
    "<br>Total population:", TOTAL,
    "<br>Young share:", scales::percent(YOUNG_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Active share:", scales::percent(ACTIVE_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Old share:", scales::percent(OLD_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Group:", Ageing_Group
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Interactive Ternary Plot of Singapore Population Structure, 2018",
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"),
    ternary = ternaryAxes,
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0.15,
      y = -0.1
    )
  )








plot_ly(
  agpop_share,
  a = ~YOUNG_SHARE,
  b = ~ACTIVE_SHARE,
  c = ~OLD_SHARE,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  color = ~Ageing_Group,
  colors = c("#2A6F6F", "#D95F02"),
  marker = list(
    size = 7,
    opacity = 0.75,
    line = list(
      color = "#1F1F1F",
      width = 0.5
    )
  ),
  text = ~paste(
    "Planning Area:", PA,
    "<br>Subzone:", SZ,
    "<br>Total population:", TOTAL,
    "<br>Young share:", scales::percent(YOUNG_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Active share:", scales::percent(ACTIVE_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Old share:", scales::percent(OLD_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Group:", Ageing_Group
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Interactive Ternary Plot of Singapore Population Structure, 2018",
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"),
    ternary = ternaryAxes,
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0.15,
      y = -0.1
    )
  )

  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8], na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16], na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21], na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24], na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(Year == 2018) %>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)

title: Hands-on_Ex06a
text:
A ternary plot places three variables on a triangular coordinate system. Every point is positioned according to the balance of the three components.
For this exercise:

the bottom-left axis represents young population;
the bottom-right axis represents active population;
the top axis represents old population.

A point closer to one corner means that the corresponding component has a higher share.


The simplest ternary plot can be created using ggtern(). In the code below, YOUNG, ACTIVE and OLD are mapped to the three ternary axes.

The plotThe code chunk



ggtern(
  data = agpop_mutated,
  aes(x = YOUNG,
      y = ACTIVE,
      z = OLD)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 1.6
  )











ggtern(
  data = agpop_mutated,
  aes(x = YOUNG,
      y = ACTIVE,
      z = OLD)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 1.6
  )




This first plot is useful as a basic check. It confirms whether the three age groups can be displayed in a ternary coordinate system.
However, the chart still needs better labels and styling before it becomes suitable for interpretation.



The next version adds a clear title and applies a cleaner ternary theme. A muted teal colour is used to keep the visual style consistent with the previous exercises.

The plotThe code chunk



ggtern(
  data = agpop_mutated,
  aes(x = YOUNG,
      y = ACTIVE,
      z = OLD)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 1.7
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population Structure of Singapore, 2018",
    subtitle = "Ternary plot of young, active and old population groups",
    T = "Young",
    L = "Active",
    R = "Old"
  ) +
  theme_rgbw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Ignoring unknown labels:
• T : "Young"
• L : "Active"
• R : "Old"












ggtern(
  data = agpop_mutated,
  aes(x = YOUNG,
      y = ACTIVE,
      z = OLD)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.65,
    size = 1.7
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population Structure of Singapore, 2018",
    subtitle = "Ternary plot of young, active and old population groups",
    T = "Young",
    L = "Active",
    R = "Old"
  ) +
  theme_rgbw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )




This plot shows how Singapore’s subzones differ in population composition. Areas with a relatively older population will move closer to the old corner, while areas with more working-age residents will be located closer to the active side.



A useful extension is to map total population to point size. This allows the plot to show both composition and relative scale.
The triangle still shows the age structure, while the point size gives a quick sense of which subzones have larger population bases.

The plotThe code chunk



ggtern(
  data = agpop_share,
  aes(x = YOUNG_SHARE,
      y = ACTIVE_SHARE,
      z = OLD_SHARE)
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(size = TOTAL),
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    name = "Total population",
    range = c(1, 5)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population Composition and Size by Singapore Subzone, 2018",
    subtitle = "Point position shows age composition; point size shows total population",
    T = "Young share",
    L = "Active share",
    R = "Old share"
  ) +
  theme_rgbw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

Ignoring unknown labels:
• T : "Young share"
• L : "Active share"
• R : "Old share"












ggtern(
  data = agpop_share,
  aes(x = YOUNG_SHARE,
      y = ACTIVE_SHARE,
      z = OLD_SHARE)
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(size = TOTAL),
    color = "#2A6F6F",
    alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    name = "Total population",
    range = c(1, 5)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Population Composition and Size by Singapore Subzone, 2018",
    subtitle = "Point position shows age composition; point size shows total population",
    T = "Young share",
    L = "Active share",
    R = "Old share"
  ) +
  theme_rgbw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.position = "right"
  )




This version is slightly more informative because it avoids treating every subzone as equally large. A small subzone and a large subzone may have similar composition, but they matter differently when interpreted from a planning perspective.



To add more analytical value, we can classify subzones by whether their old population share is above the median. This does not overcomplicate the analysis, but it makes the ternary plot easier to interpret.

old_share_median <- median(agpop_share$OLD_SHARE, na.rm = TRUE)

agpop_share <- agpop_share %>%
  mutate(
    Ageing_Group = if_else(
      OLD_SHARE >= old_share_median,
      "Higher old-age share",
      "Lower old-age share"
    )
  )


The plotThe code chunk



ggtern(
  data = agpop_share,
  aes(x = YOUNG_SHARE,
      y = ACTIVE_SHARE,
      z = OLD_SHARE)
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = Ageing_Group),
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Higher old-age share" = "#D95F02",
      "Lower old-age share" = "#2A6F6F"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ternary Plot of Age Structure by Old-age Share",
    subtitle = "Subzones are grouped by whether old-age share is above or below the median",
    T = "Young share",
    L = "Active share",
    R = "Old share",
    color = "Ageing group"
  ) +
  theme_rgbw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

Ignoring unknown labels:
• T : "Young share"
• L : "Active share"
• R : "Old share"












old_share_median <- median(agpop_share$OLD_SHARE, na.rm = TRUE)

agpop_share <- agpop_share %>%
  mutate(
    Ageing_Group = if_else(
      OLD_SHARE >= old_share_median,
      "Higher old-age share",
      "Lower old-age share"
    )
  )

ggtern(
  data = agpop_share,
  aes(x = YOUNG_SHARE,
      y = ACTIVE_SHARE,
      z = OLD_SHARE)
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = Ageing_Group),
    alpha = 0.7,
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Higher old-age share" = "#D95F02",
      "Lower old-age share" = "#2A6F6F"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ternary Plot of Age Structure by Old-age Share",
    subtitle = "Subzones are grouped by whether old-age share is above or below the median",
    T = "Young share",
    L = "Active share",
    R = "Old share",
    color = "Ageing group"
  ) +
  theme_rgbw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )




This extension makes the chart more analytical. The ternary plot no longer only shows many points inside a triangle; it also helps identify which subzones are more ageing-leaning compared with the overall median.

title: Hands-on_Ex06a
text:
The interactive ternary plot is created using plot_ly(). This allows the user to hover over each point and inspect the area name, subzone, total population and age-group shares.


The helper functions below are used to format the plot annotation and ternary axes.

label <- function(txt) {
  list(
    text = txt,
    x = 0.1,
    y = 1,
    ax = 0,
    ay = 0,
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    align = "center",
    font = list(
      family = "serif",
      size = 15,
      color = "white"
    ),
    bgcolor = "#2A6F6F",
    bordercolor = "#1F1F1F",
    borderwidth = 2
  )
}

axis <- function(txt) {
  list(
    title = txt,
    tickformat = ".0%",
    tickfont = list(size = 10)
  )
}

ternaryAxes <- list(
  aaxis = axis("Young"),
  baxis = axis("Active"),
  caxis = axis("Old")
)





The plotThe code chunk



plot_ly(
  agpop_share,
  a = ~YOUNG_SHARE,
  b = ~ACTIVE_SHARE,
  c = ~OLD_SHARE,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  color = ~Ageing_Group,
  colors = c("#2A6F6F", "#D95F02"),
  marker = list(
    size = 7,
    opacity = 0.75,
    line = list(
      color = "#1F1F1F",
      width = 0.5
    )
  ),
  text = ~paste(
    "Planning Area:", PA,
    "<br>Subzone:", SZ,
    "<br>Total population:", TOTAL,
    "<br>Young share:", scales::percent(YOUNG_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Active share:", scales::percent(ACTIVE_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Old share:", scales::percent(OLD_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Group:", Ageing_Group
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Interactive Ternary Plot of Singapore Population Structure, 2018",
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"),
    ternary = ternaryAxes,
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0.15,
      y = -0.1
    )
  )








plot_ly(
  agpop_share,
  a = ~YOUNG_SHARE,
  b = ~ACTIVE_SHARE,
  c = ~OLD_SHARE,
  type = "scatterternary",
  mode = "markers",
  color = ~Ageing_Group,
  colors = c("#2A6F6F", "#D95F02"),
  marker = list(
    size = 7,
    opacity = 0.75,
    line = list(
      color = "#1F1F1F",
      width = 0.5
    )
  ),
  text = ~paste(
    "Planning Area:", PA,
    "<br>Subzone:", SZ,
    "<br>Total population:", TOTAL,
    "<br>Young share:", scales::percent(YOUNG_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Active share:", scales::percent(ACTIVE_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Old share:", scales::percent(OLD_SHARE, accuracy = 0.1),
    "<br>Group:", Ageing_Group
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Interactive Ternary Plot of Singapore Population Structure, 2018",
    annotations = label("Ternary Markers"),
    ternary = ternaryAxes,
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0.15,
      y = -0.1
    )
  )




The interactive version is useful because the ternary plot may contain many overlapping points. Hover information allows the chart to remain clean while still showing detailed information for each subzone.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
This report addresses the ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1 requirement: apply visual analytics for data discovery to a motor vehicle insurance portfolio. The analytical aim is not merely to describe the dataset. It is to identify where profitability and volatility differ across policy, customer, vehicle and exposure characteristics.
This report deliberately uses an independent visual pathway for Cheng Yuanyuan’s submission. It emphasises distribution shape, concentration, exposure-aware comparison, binned density and interaction diagnostics, so the analytical argument is not dependent on a single chart family or a single segment-ranking approach.









Requirement area
How this report addresses it




Data wrangling
Imports the actual CSV and data dictionary; cleans names; audits missingness, duplicates, exposure and variable types; engineers loss-ratio, claim-frequency, severity and capped distribution variables.


Univariate visual analytics
Uses ECDFs, zero-outcome shares, density views and capped-distribution diagnostics for premium, incurred loss and loss ratio.


Bivariate visual analytics
Compares profitability and volatility by product, bonus, payment, business type, brand and vehicle characteristics, including distribution-shape and interaction diagnostics.


Visual communication
Uses chart types that match the data structure: indexed trends, ECDF, Pareto curve, binned heatmap, lollipop chart, violin/boxplot, funnel plot and interaction heatmap.


Reproducibility
All data import, processing, chart and test code is included and folded under clickable Code controls.


Bonus / additional methods
Applies ECDF, Pareto concentration, funnel comparison, two-way heatmap and distribution-shape diagnostics beyond basic bar charts.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
4.1 Exposure, premium and incurred-loss distribution


Code
p1 <- motor %>%
  filter(total_premium >= 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = log1p(total_premium))) +
  stat_ecdf(geom = "step", color = my_blue_dark, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "ECDF of log premium", x = "log(1 + total premium)", y = "Cumulative share") +
  base_theme

p2 <- motor %>%
  filter(total_incurred >= 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = log1p(total_incurred))) +
  stat_ecdf(geom = "step", color = my_accent, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "ECDF of log incurred loss", x = "log(1 + total incurred)", y = "Cumulative share") +
  base_theme

p1 | p2









ECDF charts are used because insurance outcomes are not symmetric. They show distribution position and tail behaviour without requiring the data to be normally distributed.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
4.2 Zero outcomes and right-tail concentration


Code
zero_plot <- tibble(
  category = c("Zero claims", "Zero incurred loss"),
  share = c(portfolio_total$zero_claim_share, portfolio_total$zero_loss_share)
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = share)) +
  geom_col(fill = my_blue, color = my_dark, width = 0.55) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.25, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Zero outcome share", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  base_theme

pareto_loss <- motor %>%
  filter(total_incurred > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(total_incurred)) %>%
  mutate(
    row_share = row_number() / n(),
    loss_share = cumsum(total_incurred) / sum(total_incurred)
  )

pareto_plot <- pareto_loss %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = row_share, y = loss_share)) +
  geom_line(color = my_blue_dark, linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Pareto curve of incurred loss", x = "Cumulative share of positive-loss records", y = "Cumulative share of incurred loss") +
  base_theme

zero_plot | pareto_plot









The Pareto view is particularly relevant to volatility because it shows whether portfolio loss is generated by many moderate claims or by a relatively small adverse tail.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
5.1 Indexed time movement


Code
portfolio_year %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  transmute(
    year,
    `Premium per exposure` = premium_rate / first(premium_rate) * 100,
    `Incurred per exposure` = incurred_rate / first(incurred_rate) * 100,
    `Claim frequency` = claim_frequency / first(claim_frequency) * 100,
    `Loss ratio` = loss_ratio / first(loss_ratio) * 100
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "metric", values_to = "index") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = index, color = metric, group = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(portfolio_year$year))) +
  labs(title = "Indexed movement of key portfolio metrics", x = NULL, y = "Index, first year = 100", color = NULL) +
  base_theme









Indexing allows metrics with different units to be compared on the same chart. This is more informative than putting premium, incurred losses and claim counts on separate unrelated scales.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
5.2 Premium versus incurred loss


Code
motor %>%
  filter(total_premium > 0, total_incurred >= 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = premium_log, y = incurred_log)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 45) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#EAF2FB", high = my_blue_dark, labels = comma) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = my_accent, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Binned relationship between premium and incurred loss", x = "log(1 + total premium)", y = "log(1 + total incurred)", fill = "Policy-years") +
  base_theme









A binned heatmap is selected because the dataset is too large for a readable raw scatterplot. The chart identifies dense areas where premium and incurred loss are misaligned.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
5.3 Product profitability and exposure importance


Code
product_display <- policy_type_summary %>%
  filter(exposure >= 100) %>%
  mutate(segment = fct_reorder(segment, loss_ratio))

p_prod_lr <- product_display %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = segment, y = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = segment, y = 0, yend = loss_ratio), color = my_blue_light, linewidth = 4) +
  geom_point(color = my_blue_dark, size = 4) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Portfolio loss ratio by product", x = NULL, y = NULL) + base_theme

p_prod_mix <- product_display %>%
  mutate(exposure_share = exposure / sum(exposure)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(segment, exposure_share), y = exposure_share)) +
  geom_col(fill = my_blue, color = my_dark, width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Exposure share by product", x = NULL, y = NULL) + base_theme

p_prod_lr | p_prod_mix









The lollipop chart emphasises ranking while reducing the visual weight of bars. Showing exposure share beside loss ratio prevents overreaction to small products.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
5.4 Bonus-score distribution and frequency


Code
p_bonus_dist <- motor %>%
  filter(is.finite(lr_cap_95), total_exposure > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bonus_score, y = lr_cap_95, fill = bonus_score)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.55, color = my_dark, linewidth = 0.25, trim = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.18, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(my_blue_light, my_blue, my_blue_dark, "#9EC1E6")) +
  labs(title = "Capped loss-ratio distribution by bonus score", x = NULL, y = "Loss ratio, capped at 95th percentile") + base_theme

p_bonus_freq <- bonus_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(segment, claim_frequency), y = claim_frequency)) +
  geom_col(fill = my_blue, color = my_dark, width = 0.65) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Claim frequency by bonus score", x = NULL, y = "Claims / exposure") + base_theme

p_bonus_dist | p_bonus_freq









The violin-plus-boxplot combination is used because bonus-score risk is distributional. It shows whether one group has a wider adverse tail, not only a different average.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
5.5 Payment frequency and business-type interaction


Code
pay_business <- motor %>%
  filter(total_exposure > 0) %>%
  group_by(payment_frequency, business_type) %>%
  summarise(
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

pay_business %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = payment_frequency, y = business_type, fill = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#D7E6F5", high = my_blue_dark, labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Loss ratio by payment frequency and business type", x = "Payment frequency", y = "Business type", fill = "Loss ratio") +
  base_theme +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())









This heatmap is used because payment frequency and business type may interact. It avoids the misleading implication that a single variable explains all observed risk.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
5.6 Vehicle-brand funnel plot


Code
brand_funnel <- brand_summary %>%
  filter(exposure >= 50, is.finite(loss_ratio)) %>%
  mutate(
    expected_lr = portfolio_total$loss_ratio,
    se = sqrt(pmax(expected_lr * (1 - pmin(expected_lr, 0.99)), 0.0001) / exposure),
    upper_band = expected_lr + 1.96 * se,
    lower_band = pmax(expected_lr - 1.96 * se, 0),
    outlier = loss_ratio > upper_band
  )

brand_funnel %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = exposure, y = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = outlier), size = 2.7, alpha = 0.82) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = portfolio_total$loss_ratio, linetype = "dashed", color = my_dark) +
  geom_line(aes(y = upper_band), color = my_accent, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = lower_band), color = my_accent, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = my_blue, "TRUE" = "#D62728")) +
  labs(title = "Funnel plot of vehicle-brand loss ratio", x = "Brand exposure, log scale", y = "Loss ratio", color = "Above band") +
  base_theme









The funnel plot addresses a common visual analytics error: ranking segments without considering segment size. It is a more defensible way to screen brand outliers.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
text:
5.7 Vehicle value and power-to-weight interaction


Code
vehicle_heat <- motor %>%
  filter(!is.na(vehicle_value_band), !is.na(power_band), total_exposure > 0) %>%
  group_by(vehicle_value_band, power_band) %>%
  summarise(
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(exposure >= 100)

vehicle_heat %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = vehicle_value_band, y = power_band, fill = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 1)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#D7E6F5", high = my_blue_dark, labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Loss ratio by vehicle value and power-to-weight", x = "Vehicle value band", y = "Power-to-weight band", fill = "Loss ratio") +
  base_theme +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())









This heatmap is more informative than separate one-variable charts because it detects risk pockets created by combinations.

title: ISSS608 Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Motor Insurance Profitability and Volatility
section: 5.8 Distribution-shape diagnostics for product and bonus groups
text:
5.8 Distribution-shape diagnostics for product and bonus groups
The executive summary includes a distribution-shape add-on because the insurance outcome is highly zero-heavy and right-skewed. A standard mean bar chart compresses this structure into one number and hides whether a segment is consistently adverse or merely affected by a small number of extreme policies. The technical report therefore adds two complementary diagnostics:

Density of capped loss ratio by product type: this evaluates whether products differ in the overall shape of profitability outcomes after extreme values are capped at the 95th percentile.
Quantile profile by bonus score: this evaluates whether bonus groups diverge only at the median or also in the upper tail, which is more relevant for volatility and adverse-risk management.

The loss ratio is capped only for visualisation. The raw loss_ratio and portfolio-weighted segment metrics remain available in the prepared dataset. Capping is used because otherwise a small number of extreme claim outcomes would dominate the x-axis and make the main distribution unreadable.


Code
p_product_density <- motor %>%
  filter(is.finite(lr_cap_95), total_exposure > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = lr_cap_95, color = policy_type)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1, adjust = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Capped loss-ratio density by product type",
    subtitle = "Density comparison shows whether product risk differs by shape, not only by average",
    x = "Loss ratio, capped at 95th percentile",
    y = "Density",
    color = "Product type"
  ) +
  base_theme

bonus_quantile_profile <- motor %>%
  filter(is.finite(lr_cap_95), total_exposure > 0, !is.na(bonus_score)) %>%
  group_by(bonus_score) %>%
  summarise(
    q25 = quantile(lr_cap_95, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(lr_cap_95, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(lr_cap_95, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    q90 = quantile(lr_cap_95, 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(-bonus_score, names_to = "quantile", values_to = "loss_ratio") %>%
  mutate(quantile = factor(quantile, levels = c("q25", "median", "q75", "q90")))

p_bonus_quantile <- bonus_quantile_profile %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = quantile, y = loss_ratio, group = bonus_score, color = bonus_score)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Capped loss-ratio quantile profile by bonus score",
    subtitle = "Quantile lines reveal where group differences appear across the distribution",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Capped loss ratio",
    color = "Bonus score"
  ) +
  base_theme

p_product_density | p_bonus_quantile









Interpretation. The density plot is appropriate because the analytical question is about shape: whether products have different concentrations of low-loss and adverse-loss records. The quantile profile is appropriate because bonus groups may look similar at the lower part of the distribution but separate in the upper tail. Together, these views support the executive conclusion that pricing review should not rely only on average loss ratio.
